annotations.source_pub: Plutarch's Lives, tr. Aubrey Stewart & George Long, vol. 4 (London, 1892 printing) (PD)
annotations.quote:
During the campaign all the daytime when he was not with Pompeius he was
employed about study and books; and not only at other times, but also
before the great battle. It was the height of summer, and the heat was
excessive, as they were encamped close to marshy ground; and those who
carried the tent of Brutus did not come quickly. After being much
harassed about these matters, and having scarcely by midday anointed
himself and taken a little to eat, while the rest were either sleeping
or engaged in thought and care about the future, he kept on writing till
evening-time, making an epitome of Polybius.
annotations.note: On the eve of Pharsalus in 48 BC, with the Republic's fate about to be settled, the man who would help kill Caesar four years later spent a sweltering afternoon abridging Polybius. Plutarch tells it as a portrait of the scholar-soldier, but beside this chapter it reads as something sharper: a Roman in the middle of a civil war, reaching for the book that explained how Rome came to rule the world, and taking literally Polybius' promise that history teaches us to bear changes of fortune. The epitome itself is lost.

annotations.source_pub: The Federalist Papers (Project Gutenberg text of the 1787-88 essays) (PD)
annotations.quote:
The Achaean league, as it is called, was another society of Grecian
republics, which supplies us with valuable instruction. ... It appears
that the cities had all the same laws and customs, the same weights and
measures, and the same money. ... It is much to be regretted that such
imperfect monuments remain of this curious political fabric. Could its
interior structure and regular operation be ascertained, it is probable
that more light would be thrown by it on the science of federal
government, than by any of the like experiments with which we are
acquainted.
annotations.note: Writing as "Publius" in December 1787, Madison went looking for a federal republic that had worked and found the Achaean League, whose story survives chiefly because Polybius, the son of an Achaean general, told it. "The same weights and measures, and the same money" is Polybius' own detail from this chapter (2.37). Madison's regret over the "imperfect monuments" is partly a regret over this book's own losses: the later books that followed the League to its end survive only in fragments.

annotations.work: Discourses on the First Decade of Titus Livius, I.2
annotations.source_pub: Discourses on the First Decade of Titus Livius, tr. Ninian Hill Thomson (London, 1883) (PD)
annotations.quote:
Other, and, as many have thought, wiser teachers, will have it, that
there are altogether six forms of government, three of them utterly bad,
the other three good in themselves, but so readily corrupted that they
too are apt to become hurtful. ... For this is the circle revolving
within which all States are and have been governed ... Wise legislators
therefore, knowing these defects, and avoiding each of these forms in
its simplicity, have made choice of a form which shares in the qualities
of all the first three, and which they judge to be more stable and
lasting than any of these separately. For where we have a monarchy, an
aristocracy, and a democracy existing together in the same city, each of
the three serves as a check upon the other.
annotations.note: Machiavelli never names his source; the six forms and their cycle come from "other, and, as many have thought, wiser teachers." The teacher is Polybius, and the chapter follows his Book 6 argument step by step: the herd choosing the strongest, the birth of justice from anger at ingratitude, each good form sliding into its corrupt twin, and the escape into a mixed constitution on the model of Lycurgus. Machiavelli even keeps Polybius' twist about Rome (6.10): what Sparta got from one man's foresight, Rome reached through struggle, or, as he puts it, "obtained by chance."
